Encrypted Neural Networks without Overflows

Philipp Kern Affiliation: Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, Germany Email: philipp.kern@kit.edu    Lorenzo Rovida Affiliation: Polytechnic University of Turin, Italy Email: teuber@kit.edu    Samuel Teuber Affiliation: Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, Germany Email: lorenzo.rovida@polito.it    Edoardo Manino Affiliation: The University of Manchester, UK Email: edoardo.manino@manchester.ac.uk    Carsten Sinz Affiliation: Karlsruhe University of Applied Sciences, Germany Email: carsten.sinz@h-ka.de    Alberto Leporati Affiliation: University of Milano-Bicocca, Italy Email: alberto.leporati@unimib.it*-0.5mm
Abstract

Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) enables private inference by evaluating neural networks on encrypted data. In this way, we can delegate the computation to a third party server without ever revealing the user’s data. Currently, the CKKS scheme is the backbone of most efficient FHE implementations, but it only supports addition, multiplication, and array rotation operations, thus requiring all activation functions of the neural network to be approximated by polynomials within a certain interval, imposing strict design tolerances. In this paper, we demonstrate for the first time that this scheme is vulnerable to overflow attacks, i.e., seemingly benign inputs that can exceed such tolerances of the FHE circuit, thereby causing corrupt and unusable outputs. To avoid them, we propose a formal verification technique that computes certified bounds on the ranges of all neurons in the network. By construction, our method eliminates overflows and, in our experiments, removed observed overflows on all benchmarks, reducing failure rates from up to 47% to 0%. Moreover, our overflow-free solution is compatible with most CKKS-based frameworks, as it allows to simply substitute standard polynomials by polynomials with rigorously designed ranges.

1 Introduction

Private inference schemes based on fully-homomorphic encryption (FHE) are designed to delegate the bulk of the computation to a third-party, without revealing the data itself [1]. This is especially relevant for the so-called machine learning as a service (MLaaS) business model, where clients buy access to a machine learning model, and run it on third-party servers [2]. An ideal FHE private inference scheme would encrypt the client data before transmission to the server, run the full inference over encrypted data, and only decrypt the output once it is transmitted back to the client.That way, the third-party server does never access the plaintext data, which might contain personal information.11 1 The honest-but-curious threat model for the third-party server is a staple of the private inference literature.

Several FHE schemes have been designed to realise this vision, including BGV [3], BFV [4, 5], and TFHE [6]. Among them, the CKKS scheme [7] has emerged as the de facto standard for efficiently implementing private neural inference, as it allows to natively encode vectors of complex numbers and perform massive arithmetic operations in parallel. Recent work demonstrates that executing deep convolutional networks [8] and large language models [9, 10] with CKKS is possible. However, the CKKS scheme imposes severe restrictions on the arithmetic operations available over the ciphertext: it only supports addition, multiplication, and array rotation. Thus, existing CKKS inference frameworks replace non-linear activation functions in the network with (high degree) polynomials [11, 12].

In this paper, we posit the existence of a major weakness in modern CKKS designs for neural networks (NNs): adversarial input perturbations can make the CKKS network arbitrarily diverge from its reference plaintext implementation. This is because the polynomial approximations of non-linear activation functions are only tight for a limited range of values [13, 14]. Input perturbations, adversarial or not, that exceed the range of a single activation can cause a cascade of overflows through the CKKS circuit yielding unrecoverable output values. We call this phenomenon an overflow attack22 2 We understand overflow attacks similar to adversarial attacks, not in the sense of cryptographic attacks. (see Figure 1).

Contributions.

To address this challenge, we introduce a framework for the certified design of FHE NNs. Our framework guarantees the absence of overflow attacks, while keeping the size of the FHE circuit as small as possible. In detail, we propose the following contributions:

  • •

    We present an efficient algorithm to find inputs that exceed the expected ranges of NNs with polynomial activations. With it, we demonstrate that the modern design of CKKS NNs is vulnerable to overflows. Our empirical result shows that even a small perturbation can cause up to 47%47\% of the tested inputs for a CIFAR10 NN to fail.

  • •

    To mitigate this, we introduce a differential verification framework that can programmatically compute certified bounds on the value range of all neurons in the NN and on the approximation error of the output. The framework can handle both analytic (e.g. GELU) and non-analytic activation functions (e.g. ReLU), fully-connected and convolutional layers.

  • •

    We give theoretical proofs that our bounds are sound for any possible input, i.e. not just small adversarial perturbations, and thus can be used at design time to eliminate the possibility of overflows. We also show that NNs with analytical activation functions (e.g. GELUs) yield an asymptotically smaller approximation error than NNs with non-analytical ones (e.g. ReLUs). This gives theoretical grounding to a recent empirical observation reported in [12].

  • •

    We further improve the design of CKKS NNs by allowing for the polynomial activations of different neurons in the same layer to be different, as opposed to uniform approximations in existing work. We thus generalize the Paterson-Stockmeyer algorithm [15, 16] from evaluating (ciphertext ×\times constant) to (ciphertext ×\times plaintext). Our implementation shows that our design can achieve at least a 10x reduction in error compared to the established non-certified pipelines.

We also provide an open-source implementation of our framework, based on OpenFHE [17], which includes construction of certified polynomials and conversion to CKKS NNs.

2 Background

State-of-the-art FHE NNs, especially those based on the CKKS scheme, are typically constructed in a multi-stage process, as shown in the upper part of Figure 2: A regular NN is first approximated with polynomial activations, after which the corresponding FHE circuit is built. Throughout the paper we will conversely describe our approach, which is illustrated in the lower part of the same figure.

2.1 Encrypted Computation with CKKS

We will now provide a high-level description of the CKKS scheme and defer a larger overview on FHE schemes to Appendix A.

Definition 2.1 (Arithmetic Circuit).

Given a ring RR, an arithmetic circuit (or simply circuit) is a directed acyclic graph whose nodes compute additions and multiplications from inputs, constants, and other nodes. With nn input nodes and mm output nodes, the circuit computes a function C:Rn→RmC:R^{n}\rightarrow R^{m}.

The CKKS scheme.

In the CKKS scheme, let N=2kN=2^{k} for some integer k>0k>0 and let Q>1Q>1 be a large modulus. A plaintext message 𝐱∈ℂN/2\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{C}^{N/2} is first encoded as a polynomial (using a scaled inverse Fourier transform), then a small random error is introduced to ensure security. This results in a slightly perturbed message 𝐱+𝒆CKKS​(𝐱)∈ℂN/2\mathbf{x}+{\bm{e}}_{\text{CKKS}}(\mathbf{x})\in\mathbb{C}^{N/2}, which is finally encrypted modulo QQ.

Like all standard FHE schemes, CKKS is based on the hardness of the Ring-Learning With Errors (RLWE) problem [18] that requires an injection of random noise during encryption to ensure security. With noisy inputs, each homomorphic operation introduces additional noise into the ciphertext, with multiplications contributing most significantly. To manage this, CKKS uses: (i) a scaling factor Δ\Delta, which controls the numerical precision by encrypting Δ​𝐱+𝒆\Delta\mathbf{x}+{\bm{e}}, and (ii) a modulus chain Q=∏i=1ℓqiQ=\prod_{i=1}^{\ell}q_{i}, with qi≈Δq_{i}\approx\Delta, which limits the number of sequential multiplications to reduce the scale back to Δ\Delta after a multiplication (whose result has scale OPENΔ2)\Delta^{2}). This technique implies that the depth of circuits that can be evaluated without additional techniques (such as bootstrapping [19]) is bounded.

CKKS decryption requires intermediate values to remain in a bounded range. If the magnitude of the underlying plaintext exceeds half the available modulus, the ciphertext may become undecodable, leading to corrupted outputs. This makes range management a central challenge in CKKS circuit design. In CKKS, as explained above, standard non-linear activation functions such as ReLU or GELU must be replaced by polynomial approximations. The accuracy of such approximations depends critically on the input range over which they are evaluated. If intermediate values exceed the expected range, approximation errors grow rapidly (see Figure 3) and may ultimately yield arithmetic overflows. Ensuring that all intermediate values remain within certified bounds is therefore essential for reliable encrypted inference, and forms the basis of our approach.

Formally, the CKKS scheme evaluates an arithmetic circuit CC as follows (details on how encrypted operations are performed can be found in Appendix B):

Definition 2.2 (CKKS Circuit [7]).

Under the CKKS encryption scheme (𝖪𝖾𝗒𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖤𝗇𝖼,𝖣𝖾𝖼,𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅)(\mathsf{KeyGen},\mathsf{Enc},\mathsf{Dec},\mathsf{Eval}), a CKKS circuit is an arithmetic circuit CC with operations 𝖠𝖣𝖣\mathsf{ADD}, 𝖬𝖴𝖫𝖳\mathsf{MULT} and 𝖱𝖮𝖳\mathsf{ROT} (for rotate), evaluated on encrypted inputs via fCKKS​(𝐱):=𝖣𝖾𝖼⁡(𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅⁡(C,𝖤𝗇𝖼⁡(𝐱))CLOSE.f_{\text{CKKS}}(\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}}):=\mathsf{Dec}(\mathsf{Eval}(C,\mathsf{Enc}(\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}})). The output satisfies fCKKS​(𝐱)=C⁡(𝐱)+eCKKS​(𝐱)f_{\text{CKKS}}(\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}})=C(\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}})+e_{\text{CKKS}}(\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}}), where eCKKS​(𝐱)e_{\text{CKKS}}(\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}}) captures the accumulated error in the output of the circuit.

2.2 Polynomial Networks

We can interpret NNs as arithmetic circuits. As CKKS only supports additions, multiplications and array rotations, we also define polynomial NNs that approximate standard NNs:

Definition 2.3 (Feed-Forward Neural Network).

A neural network computes a function f:ℐ→ℝOf:\mathcal{I}\to\mathbb{R}^{O} that maps vectors from the II-dimensional input space ℐ⊆ℝI\mathcal{I}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{I} to an OO-dimensional output space. A feed-forward architecture is a composition of layers l∈[1,L]l\in[1,L] defined as 𝐳(l)=σ(l)​(𝐳~(l))=σ(l)​(W(l)​𝐳(l−1)+𝐛(l))\mathbf{z}^{(l)}=\sigma^{(l)}\left(\tilde{\mathbf{z}}^{(l)}\right)=\sigma^{(l)}\left(W^{(l)}\mathbf{z}^{(l-1)}+\mathbf{b}^{(l)}\right) where σ(l)\sigma^{(l)} is an activation function, 𝐱=𝐳(0)∈ℐ\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{z}^{(0)}\in\mathcal{I} is the network input, and 𝐳(L)∈ℝO\mathbf{z}^{(L)}\in\mathbb{R}^{O} the network output. We denote by f(l)​(𝐱)f^{(l)}\left(\mathbf{x}\right) the value of 𝐳~(l)\tilde{\mathbf{z}}^{(l)} at layer ll for input 𝐱\mathbf{x}.

Definition 2.4 (Polynomial Neural Network).

A polynomial neural network computes a function fπ:ℐ→ℝOf_{\pi}:\mathcal{I}\to\mathbb{R}^{O} obtained from a neural network f:ℐ→ℝOf:\mathcal{I}\to\mathbb{R}^{O} by replacing the activation functions σ(l)\sigma^{(l)} in Definition 2.3 by their polynomial approximation counterparts π(l)\pi^{(l)} (see Sec. 4.1 for their construction). To differentiate the two networks, we rename the pre- and post-activation vectors from 𝐳\boldsymbol{\mathbf{z}} to 𝐲\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}, i.e. 𝐲(l)=π(l)​(𝐲~(l))=π(l)​(W(l)​𝐲(l−1)+𝐛(l))\mathbf{y}^{(l)}=\pi^{(l)}\left(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}^{(l)}\right)=\pi^{(l)}\left(W^{(l)}\mathbf{y}^{(l-1)}+\mathbf{b}^{(l)}\right) with 𝐲(0)=𝐳(0)\mathbf{y}^{(0)}=\mathbf{z}^{(0)} and 𝐲(l)≈𝐳(l)\mathbf{y}^{(l)}\approx\mathbf{z}^{(l)} for all layers l>0l>0. We call fπ(l)​(𝐱)f_{\pi}^{(l)}\left(\mathbf{x}\right) the value of 𝐲~(l)\tilde{\mathbf{y}}^{(l)} for input 𝐱\mathbf{x}.

With these approximations we can differentiate two different sources of error that influence the CKKS circuit’s output fCKKS​(𝐱)f_{\text{CKKS}}(\mathbf{x}) with respect to the output computed by the original neural network f⁡(𝐱)f(\mathbf{x}):

fCKKS​(𝐱)=fπ​(𝐱)+𝒆CKKS​(𝐱)=f⁡(𝐱)+𝒆π​(𝐱)+𝒆CKKS​(𝐱).f_{\text{CKKS}}(\mathbf{x})=f_{\pi}(\mathbf{x})+{\bm{e}}_{\text{CKKS}}(\mathbf{x})=f(\mathbf{x})+{\bm{e}}_{\pi}(\mathbf{x})+{\bm{e}}_{\text{CKKS}}(\mathbf{x})\kern 5.0pt. (1)

Here, 𝒆π​(𝐱)=fπ​(𝐱)−f⁡(𝐱){\bm{e}}_{\pi}(\mathbf{x})=f_{\pi}(\mathbf{x})-f(\mathbf{x}) is the deterministic polynomial approximation error stemming from the approximate representation of activation functions in fπf_{\pi}, while the error term 𝒆CKKS​(𝐱){\bm{e}}_{\text{CKKS}}(\mathbf{x}) is stochastic in nature and stems from the cryptographic procedures of CKKS (and RLWE encryption). The polynomial approximation error 𝒆π{\bm{e}}_{\pi} in Eq. (1) can be reduced by using higher-degree polynomials, at the cost of more multiplicative depth in the CKKS circuit and thus an increase in latency [11].

2.3 Range Estimation

To construct accurate polynomial approximations for activation functions, we must bound the range of the activation’s input (i.e. its pre-activation values). Therefore, we need to identify intervals [𝐥(l),𝐮(l)][\boldsymbol{\mathbf{l}}^{(l)},\boldsymbol{\mathbf{u}}^{(l)}] for each layer ll such that fπ(l)​(𝐱)∈[𝐥(l),𝐮(l)]f_{\pi}^{(l)}(\mathbf{x})\in[\boldsymbol{\mathbf{l}}^{(l)},\boldsymbol{\mathbf{u}}^{(l)}] is satisfied for all inputs 𝐱∈ℐ\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{I}. If there exist inputs 𝐱\mathbf{x} where fπ(l)​(𝐱)f_{\pi}^{(l)}(\mathbf{x}) is not in the computed approximation interval, the approximation may result in large errors and uncontrollable growth, eventually leading to arithmetic failures. This phenomenon is visible in the GELU\mathrm{GELU} approximation in Figure 3 which is precise for the range [−3,3]\left[-3,3\right], but diverges outside.

Sampling-based design.

The most common approach to compute ranges is based on observations from a dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D} sampled from the training data distribution. For intermediate layers ll, bounds 𝐥(l),𝐮(l)\mathbf{l}^{(l)},\mathbf{u}^{(l)} are computed, such that 𝐥(l)≤f(l)​(𝐱)≤𝐮(l)\mathbf{l}^{(l)}\leq f^{(l)}\left(\mathbf{x}\right)\leq\mathbf{u}^{(l)} holds for all 𝐱∈𝒟\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{D}. Sampling-based estimates provide no guarantees outside the dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D} and may significantly underestimate the true ranges. As a result, inputs that are out-of-distribution – or perturbed – can easily violate these ranges.

Existing countermeasures include extending sampled ranges by a factor of two [12] or choosing a constant range of [−c,c][-c,c] for a suitable constant c>0c>0 [20]. Others propose to reduce the impact of outliers on ranges by pre-multiplying the weights by orthogonal matrices [10]. We show that range violations due to sampling-based designs can lead to catastrophic failures in CKKS NNs.

3 Overflow Attacks on CKKS Networks

Computing 𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅⁡(fπ,𝖤𝗇𝖼⁡(𝐱))\mathsf{Eval}(f_{\pi},\mathsf{Enc}(\mathbf{x})) over encrypted data is a total function which always returns some value. Whether such value approximately matches the expected result is discovered only at decryption time. We say that a decryption fails if the norm of the underlying plaintext is larger than half the modulus; this induces a wrap around the modulus yielding almost randomly looking results. To emphasize the latter, we propose an extended definition of CKKS NNs which makes decryption failures explicit:

Definition 3.1 (CKKS Network with Failure Semantics).

We modify the definition of CKKS networks such that the output function’s range includes an additional value, ⊥\bot, which indicates failure of the computation. We call the modified function fCKKS⊥:ℐ→ℝO∪{⊥}f^{\bot}_{\text{CKKS}}:\mathcal{I}\rightarrow\R^{O}\cup\,\{\bot\}.

While the output of fCKKS⊥​(𝐱)f^{\bot}_{\text{CKKS}}(\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}}) is stochastic, due to the cryptographic noise 𝒆CKKS{\bm{e}}_{\text{CKKS}}, we aim to check whether there exist inputs 𝐱∈ℐ\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{I} that almost always cause a corrupt output fCKKS⊥(𝐱)=⊥f^{\bot}_{\text{CKKS}}(\mathbf{x})=\bot. We posit the existence of overflow attacks which induce failures (i.e. fCKKS⊥(𝐱)=⊥f^{\bot}_{\text{CKKS}}\left(\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}}\right)=\bot) with high probability:

Definition 3.2 (Attacks and Robustness).

Let fπ:ℐ→ℝOf_{\pi}:\mathcal{I}\to\mathbb{R}^{O} be a polynomial network with expected ranges [𝐥(l),𝐮(l)][\mathbf{l}^{(l)},\mathbf{u}^{(l)}] for all layers ll. An input 𝐱∈ℐ\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}}\in\mathcal{I} is an overflow attack on fπf_{\pi} iff there is a layer ll where fπ(l)​(𝐱)∉[𝐥(l),𝐮(l)]f^{(l)}_{\pi}\left(\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}}\right)\not\in[\mathbf{l}^{(l)},\mathbf{u}^{(l)}]. The network fπf_{\pi} is overflow robust (on ℐ\mathcal{I}) if no overflow attacks on fπf_{\pi} exist.

As the polynomial functions used for activation function approximation are typically only well-behaved on the interval [𝐥(l),𝐮(l)]\left[\mathbf{l}^{(l)},\mathbf{u}^{(l)}\right] (see also Figure 3 and Section 2.3), inputs outside this range typically induce large-scale deviations between ff and fπf_{\pi} which yield arithmetical errors. Indeed, as we show below, such inputs can easily be constructed.

Finding overflows.

To uncover vulnerabilities in CKKS NNs that are not overflow robust, we leverage classic techniques from adversarial example generation: For a given input 𝐱∈ℐ\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{I} we generate random noise 𝜹\boldsymbol{\delta} which we use to produce a perturbed version of the input (denoted γ⁡(𝐱,𝜹)\gamma\left(\mathbf{x},\boldsymbol{\delta}\right)). We then use projected gradient descent [21] to optimize 𝜹\boldsymbol{\delta} in order to find inputs which violate the internal bound assumptions of fπf_{\pi}. As direct optimization on fπf_{\pi} is numerically instable, we optimize w.r.t. ff by pushing the internal activation values (i.e. f(l)​(𝐱)f^{(l)}\left(\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}}\right) for some inner layer ll of the NN) outside the interval used for approximation. To this end, note that the internal activation values of ff and fπf_{\pi} are tightly related (until the latter violates its bound) and thus act as a natural surrogate. Formally, we maximize the distance of internal activation values to the interval centre point (𝐮(l)+𝐥(l))/2(\mathbf{u}^{(l)}+\mathbf{l}^{(l)})/2:

∑j‖(f(l)​(γ⁡(𝐱,𝜹)))j−(𝐮j(l)+𝐥j(l))/2‖∞.\sum_{j}\left\lVert\left(f^{(l)}\left(\gamma\left(\mathbf{x},\boldsymbol{\delta}\right)\right)\right)_{j}-\left(\mathbf{u}^{(l)}_{j}+\mathbf{l}^{(l)}_{j}\right)/2\right\rVert_{\infty}.
Empirical evidence.

As we will show in Section 5.2, CKKS circuits constructed via sampled bounds are vulnerable to overflow attacks for realistic inputs (see examples for CIFAR in Figure 1).

4 Avoiding Overflows by Certified Design

Given a neural network ff, we propose a method to construct robust CKKS circuits in the sense of Definition 3.2, i.e. NNs fπf_{\pi} without overflows, while simultaneously bounding the output difference ‖fπ​(𝐱)−f⁡(𝐱)‖∞\|f_{\pi}(\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}})-f(\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}})\|_{\infty}. Our approach transforms ff into its polynomial version fπf_{\pi} by iteratively rewriting its layers. For each layer ll, we first compute provable bounds such that fπ(l)​(𝐱)∈[𝐥(l),𝐮(l)]{f^{(l)}_{\pi}\left(\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}}\right)\in[\boldsymbol{\mathbf{l}}^{(l)},\boldsymbol{\mathbf{u}}^{(l)}]} for all 𝐱∈ℐ\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}}\in\mathcal{I} (Section 4.1). Linear layers then remain unchanged while activation functions are substituted by a polynomial approximation, obtained on the fly for the interval [𝐥(l),𝐮(l)][\boldsymbol{\mathbf{l}}^{(l)},\boldsymbol{\mathbf{u}}^{(l)}] using the Remez algorithm [22]. The algorithm relies on a bound for the maximum (local) error between the activation function and its approximation (Section 4.2) which is taken into account for the range analysis in subsequent layers. We additionally leverage differential verification via zonotopes [23] to compute bounds on the difference ‖fπ(l)​(𝐱)−f(l)​(𝐱)‖∞\|f_{\pi}^{(l)}(\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}})-f^{(l)}(\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}})\|_{\infty} (Section 4.4). Furthermore, we provide a direct translation from the generated polynomial network fπf_{\pi} to a CKKS circuit (Appendix D).

4.1 Sound Range Analysis for Polynomial Networks

We construct the polynomial NN fπf_{\pi} from a given NN ff by iteratively substituting a non-linear activation function σ(l)\sigma^{(l)} in layer ll by its polynomial approximation π(l)\pi^{(l)}. We compute the latter using the Remez algorithm [22] which requires a method for computing a sound bound on |π(l)​(𝐱)−σ(l)​(𝐱)||\pi^{(l)}(\mathbf{x})-\sigma^{(l)}(\mathbf{x})| (discussed in Section 4.2) and an approximation range [𝐥(l),𝐮(l)][\boldsymbol{\mathbf{l}}^{(l)},\boldsymbol{\mathbf{u}}^{(l)}].

To compute valid ranges for fπ(l)f_{\pi}^{(l)} (beyond the first polynomial layer) it is insufficient to analyse NN ff in isolation, as its output bounds also depend on the polynomial approximation errors introduced in earlier layers. To this end, we follow the approach by Manino et al. [13]: For each activation function σ(l)\sigma^{(l)} substituted by π(l)\pi^{(l)} with |π(l)​(𝐱)−σ(l)​(𝐱)|≤ϵ(l)|\pi^{(l)}(\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}})-\sigma^{(l)}(\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}})|\leq\boldsymbol{\mathbf{\epsilon}}^{(l)}, we augment the original NN f⁡(𝐱)f\left(\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}}\right) by an input 𝜹(l)∈[−ϵ(l),ϵ(l)]\boldsymbol{\mathbf{\delta}}^{(l)}\in[-\boldsymbol{\mathbf{\epsilon}}^{(l)},\boldsymbol{\mathbf{\epsilon}}^{(l)}] modelling the perturbation which yields the relaxed NN f~​(𝐱,𝜹)\tilde{f}\left(\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}},\boldsymbol{\mathbf{\delta}}\right). We then bound layer ll by solving the following optimization problem over f~\tilde{f}:

min/max⁡𝐲~(l)s.t.\displaystyle\min/\max~~\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}}^{(l)}\quad\text{s.t. } {𝐲~(j)=W(j)​𝐲(j−1)+𝐛(j)𝐲(j)=σ(j)​(𝐲~(j))+𝜹(j),𝜹(j)∈[−ϵ(j),ϵ(j)]\displaystyle\left\{\begin{aligned} \tilde{\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}}^{(j)}&=W^{(j)}\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}^{(j-1)}+\boldsymbol{\mathbf{b}}^{(j)}\\ \boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}^{(j)}&=\sigma^{(j)}\left(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}}^{(j)}\right)+\boldsymbol{\mathbf{\delta}}^{(j)},~~\boldsymbol{\mathbf{\delta}}^{(j)}\in[-\boldsymbol{\mathbf{\epsilon}}^{(j)},\boldsymbol{\mathbf{\epsilon}}^{(j)}]\end{aligned}\right. for ​j≤l\displaystyle\text{for }j\leq l (2)

As f~\tilde{f} is a standard NN (only using activations σ(l)\sigma^{(l)} instead of polynomials π(l)\pi^{(l)}), we can use state-of-the-art NN verifiers [24] to obtain guaranteed bounds. This approach allows us to construct fπf_{\pi} in a single pass over ff with the soundness guarantee given in Theorem 4.1 (see proof on page ). Below, we describe how errors on the fπf_{\pi} are bounded locally (Section 4.2) and globally (Section 4.4). main_neurips-pratenddefaultcategory.tex

Theorem 4.1 (Soundness).

For any neural network ff with input space ℐ\mathcal{I}, the construction approach given in Section 4.1 yields a network fπf_{\pi} robust to overflow attacks on ℐ\mathcal{I} (see Definition 3.2).

4.2 Piecewise-Polynomial Overapproximation of Activation Functions

Computing bounds on the univariate approximation error π(l)​(x)−σ(l)​(x)\pi^{(l)}(x)-\sigma^{(l)}(x) is indispensable for our approach and for the Remez algorithm [22] to fit high-quality polynomial approximations. Prior work on verified approximation of ReLU⁡(x)=max⁡(0,x)\relu(x)=max(0,x) uses its piecewise linearity [14]. This allows bounding the approximation error π⁡(x)−ReLU⁡(x)\pi(x)-\relu(x) by finding the extrema of the polynomials π⁡(x)−0\pi(x)-0 for x≤0x\leq 0 and π⁡(x)−x\pi(x)-x for x≥0x\geq 0. Finding the extrema of a polynomial π⁡(x)\pi(x) in Chebyshev basis reduces to finding the eigenvalues33 3 This works assumes the correctness of numerically computed eigenvalues.of the Colleague matrix associated with its derivative dd​x​π​(x)\frac{d}{dx}\pi(x) [25]. We extend this approach to activation functions that are monotonically linear almost everywhere:

Definition 4.1 (Monotonically Linear Almost Everywhere).

A function g:ℝ→ℝg:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} is monotonically linear almost everywhere iff it has bounded total variation (see Section E.1), there are a1,a2,b1,b2∈ℝa_{1},a_{2},b_{1},b_{2}\in\mathbb{R} with limx→∞(g⁡(x)−(a1​x+b1))=limx→−∞(g⁡(x)−(a2​x+b2))=0\lim_{x\to\infty}\left(g\left(x\right)-\left(a_{1}x+b_{1}\right)\right)=\lim_{x\to-\infty}\left(g\left(x\right)-\left(a_{2}x+b_{2}\right)\right)=0 and there are c1,c2∈ℝc_{1},c_{2}\in\mathbb{R} such that g⁡(x)−(a1​x+b1)g\left(x\right)-\left(a_{1}x+b_{1}\right) (resp. g⁡(x)−(a2​x+b2)g\left(x\right)-\left(a_{2}x+b_{2}\right)) is monotonic on (−∞,c1]\left(-\infty,c_{1}\right] (resp. [c2,∞)\left[c_{2},\infty\right)).

Many activation functions (e.g. ReLU, GELU or Sigmoid) satisfy this property (see Table ). We propose to address functions σ(l)\sigma^{(l)} of this type via piecewise polynomial approximations of the form

q⁡(x)=𝟙x≤d0​(x)⋅(a1​x+b1)+∑i=1n𝟙x∈(di−1,di]​(x)⋅qi​(x)+𝟙x>dn​(x)⋅(a2​x+b2)q(x)=\mathds{1}_{x\leq d_{0}}(x)\cdot(a_{1}x+b_{1})+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathds{1}_{x\in\left(d_{i-1},d_{i}\right]}(x)\cdot q_{i}\left(x\right)+\mathds{1}_{x>d_{n}}(x)\cdot(a_{2}x+b_{2})

with known approximation error ϵq≥|q⁡(x)−σ⁡(x)|\epsilon_{q}\geq|q(x)-\sigma(x)| for all x∈ℝx\in\R (with d0≤c1,dn≥c2d_{0}\leq c_{1},d_{n}\geq c_{2}, and the indicator function 𝟙p⁡(x)​(x)∈{0,1}\mathds{1}_{p(x)}(x)\in\{0,1\} being 11 for xx iff p⁡(x)p(x)). We can then use q⁡(x)q(x) as a surrogate in the Remez algorithm to fit a polynomial π(l)​(x)≈q⁡(x)≈σ(l)​(x)\pi^{(l)}(x)\approx q(x)\approx\sigma^{(l)}(x) and bound its approximation error

|π⁡(x)−σ⁡(x)|≤|π⁡(x)−q⁡(x)|+|q⁡(x)−σ⁡(x)|≤ϵπ+ϵq,\displaystyle|\pi(x)-\sigma(x)|\leq|\pi(x)-q(x)|+|q(x)-\sigma(x)|\leq\epsilon_{\pi}+\epsilon_{q}\;, (3)

where finding ϵπ\epsilon_{\pi} reduces to n+1n+1 computations of polynomial extrema and ϵq\epsilon_{q} is a known constant.

We can always construct such a function q⁡(x)q(x) given a target tolerance ϵq\epsilon_{q}. To this end, we first find points d0≤c1,dn≥c2d_{0}\leq c_{1},d_{n}\geq c_{2} with |ai​x+bi−σ⁡(x)|≤ϵq|a_{i}x+b_{i}-\sigma(x)|\leq\epsilon_{q} via binary search. Then, we use Chebyshev approximation to find polynomials qi​(x)≈σ⁡(x)q_{i}(x)\approx\sigma(x) over partitions of [d0,dn][d_{0},d_{n}]. Given concrete qi​(x)q_{i}(x), we use interval arithmetic [26] to check if |qi​(x)−σ⁡(x)|≤ϵq|q_{i}(x)-\sigma(x)|\leq\epsilon_{q} over the interval of interest. If the target tolerance is violated, we increase the number of sub-intervals. While this last step is expensive, it only has to be computed once for each activation function.

4.3 Polynomial Activations and Smoothness of Functions

The smoother an activation σ:ℝ→ℝ\sigma:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} is, the faster its polynomial approximation error converges to zero. Trefethen et al. [25] give the following bounds for the error of degree nn Chebyshev polynomial approximations πn​(x)≈σ⁡(x)\pi_{n}(x)\approx\sigma(x) (w.l.o.g. x∈[−1,1]x\in[-1,1]): |σ⁡(x)−πn​(x)|≤4​Vπ​ν​(n−ν)ν|\sigma(x)-\pi_{n}(x)|\leq\frac{4V}{\pi\nu(n-\nu)^{\nu}} (4) |σ⁡(x)−πn​(x)|≤4​M​ρ−nρ−1|\sigma(x)-\pi_{n}(x)|\leq\frac{4M\rho^{-n}}{\rho-1} (5) Equation (4) holds, if σ\sigma is ν\nu times differentiable, n>νn>\nu and V=V[−1,1]​(σ(ν))V=V_{[-1,1]}(\sigma^{(\nu)}) is the total variation (see Appendix E.1) of the ν\nu-th derivative of σ\sigma. Equation (5) is applicable to activations that are analytic over [−1,1][-1,1] (their Taylor expansion converges to σ\sigma for any x∈[−1,1]x\in[-1,1]). Here, convergence is affected by M=maxx∈Eρ⁡|σ⁡(x)|M=\max_{x\in E_{\rho}}|\sigma(x)|, where a larger ρ\rho for the Bernstein ellipse EρE_{\rho} (see Appendix E.2) indicates that σ\sigma can be analytically continued further into the complex plane. VV and MM are independent of nn.

The first bound implies that the approximation error decays with rate O⁡(n−ν)O(n^{-\nu}), i.e. faster with the number of times σ\sigma is differentiable. If σ\sigma meets the criteria of the second bound, then the error decays at an even faster rate O⁡(ρn)O(\rho^{n}) depending on how far σ\sigma can be analytically continued into the complex plane. The effects of these bounds is visualised in Figure 4: The approximation error for the once-differentiable ELU\elu activation converges faster than the error for the non-differentiable ReLU\relu function. The errors for the analytic functions Sigm​(x)=1/(1+e−x)\text{Sigm}(x)=1/(1+e^{-x}) and SiLU⁡(x)=x⋅Sigm​(x)\silu(x)=x\cdot\text{Sigm}(x) converge much faster. While Sigm​(x)\text{Sigm}(x) and SiLU⁡(x)\silu(x) have poles at x=±π​ix=\pm\pi i, GELU⁡(x)\gelu(x) can be analytically continued to the entire complex plane. Therefore, we see even faster convergence for this activation functions – at least before convergence of the approximation error levels off due to limits of floating point accuracy. Consequently, SiLU\silu and even more so GELU\gelu makes precise polynomial approximation of neural networks easier.

4.4 Differential Bounds via Differential Verification

Construction of fπf_{\pi} according to Section 4.1 guarantees robustness, but we also desire bounds on the deviation ‖fπ​(𝐱)−f⁡(𝐱)‖∞\|f_{\pi}(\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}})-f(\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}})\|_{\infty} between the polynomial and the original NN. Prior work shows that standard verifiers struggle to tightly bound the difference between two NNs [27, 28, 23]. However, when NNs have the same architecture and similar weights, approaches for differential verification [27, 28, 29, 23] produce tighter bounds by propagating local bounds on the difference through the NN.

To this end, note that the difference 𝚫~(l)=𝐲~1(l)−𝐲~2(l)\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mathbf{\Delta}}}^{(l)}=\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}}_{1}^{(l)}-\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}}_{2}^{(l)} between two pre-activation values can be expressed in terms of the difference 𝚫(l−1)=𝐲1(l−1)−𝐲2(l−1)\boldsymbol{\mathbf{\Delta}}^{(l-1)}=\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}_{1}^{(l-1)}-\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}_{2}^{(l-1)} between the results of the previous layer via the identity 𝚫~(l)=(W1−W2)​𝐲2+W1​𝚫(l−1)+(𝐛1−𝐛2).\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mathbf{\Delta}}}^{(l)}=\left(W_{1}-W_{2}\right)\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}_{2}+W_{1}\boldsymbol{\mathbf{\Delta}}^{(l-1)}+\left(\boldsymbol{\mathbf{b}}_{1}-\boldsymbol{\mathbf{b}}_{2}\right). The post-activation difference can be similarly rewritten as 𝚫(l)=σ1(l)​(𝐲~1(l))−σ2(l)​(𝐲~2(l))=σ1(l)​(𝐲~1(l))−σ2(l)​(𝐲~1(l)−𝚫~(l))\boldsymbol{\mathbf{\Delta}}^{(l)}=\sigma^{(l)}_{1}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}}_{1}^{(l)})-\sigma^{(l)}_{2}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}}_{2}^{(l)})=\sigma^{(l)}_{1}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}}_{1}^{(l)})-\sigma^{(l)}_{2}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}}_{1}^{(l)}-\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mathbf{\Delta}}}^{(l)}).

As common for NN verifiers, differential verification also leverages linear over-approximations for activation functions. While existing work provides relaxations for the bivariate non-linearity σ1(l)​(x)−σ2(l)​(x−Δ)\sigma_{1}^{(l)}(x)-\sigma_{2}^{(l)}(x-\Delta) for σ1(l)=σ2(l)\sigma_{1}^{(l)}=\sigma_{2}^{(l)} with bounded derivative [29], it cannot handle polynomial σ1(l)\sigma_{1}^{(l)} for σ2(l)≠ReLU\sigma_{2}^{(l)}\neq\relu. Building on the relaxation by Banerjee et al. [29], we extend the differential verification tool VeryDiff [23] with parallel linear relaxations for this case (see proof on page ):

5 Experiments

Our experiments44 4 The source code is available at https://github.com/lorenzorovida/encrypted-neural-networks-without-overflows are designed to (i) evaluate the impact of each contribution on the performance of our approach (Section 5.1), (ii) show the existence of overflow attacks (Section 5.2), and (iii) demonstrate that certified design yields comparable accuracy for plaintext and encrypted inference (Section 5.3).

We evaluate on fully connected (FC) NNs trained on the HELOC (Home Equity Line of Credit) [30], MNIST [20] and EC (Energy Consumption) [31] datasets, as well as convolutional (Conv) NNs trained on CIFAR10 [32]. We further retrained FC NNs based on the NN4Sys benchmark [33] for learned index prediction and Conv NNs for remaining useful life prediction (Collins RUL) [34] taken from the annual NN verification competition VNNComp [35]. Overall, the NNs cover a wide range of sizes containing between 6464 and 1030010300 neurons.Following prior work on certified design of polynomial NNs based on ReLU\relu NNs [14], we trained all NNs with L1L_{1} regularization to encourage tighter pre-activation bounds. Experiments for plaintext NNs were run on Ubuntu with 44-Core Intel Xeon E5-1630v3 and 128128 GiB of RAM. CKKS inference on a M5 Max CPU with 3636 GiB of RAM. Additional evaluation results can be found in Appendix H.

5.1 Ablation Study

We construct polynomial NNs approximating a base NN for multiple values of the polynomial degree dd and measure the verifiable and maximally observed error (w.r.t. to the respective dataset). Comparing the error metrics between different construction settings enables us to evaluate the effect of our individual contributions. To show the effects on FC and Conv NNs, we report the results for the MNIST 4×2564\times 256 NN and the small Collins RUL NN ([1600,2400,800,600,100][1600,2400,800,600,100] neurons per layer).

GELU vs. ReLU networks. Figure 5 clearly shows that the approximation error for GELU\gelu NNs is far smaller than for NNs with ReLU\relu activation. This effect gets stronger with increasing dd.

Heterogeneous vs. uniform polynomial layers. Error values when using different polynomial activations in the same layer are significantly smaller than the uniform baseline.

Verified vs. sampled bounds. Using sampled pre-activation bounds leads to substantially smaller sampled error values. This is expected as sampled values (even if bounds are widened by a constant factor) do not suffer from overapproximation to the same extent as bounds computed using NN verification techniques. However, these polynomial NNs are prone to overflow attacks. Moreover, the above effect is only valid if we fix the activation function: When we compare the sampled error for ReLU\relu NNs with sampling-based bounds to the sampling error for GELU\gelu NNs with verified bounds, the GELU\gelu NNs achieve a better or similar approximation error already for d≤40d\leq 40 on both MNIST and Collins RUL. The effect is even more pronounced comparing ReLU\relu NNs with a single polynomial per layerand sampled bounds to verified GELU\gelu NNs with multiple polynomials per layer.

5.2 Vulnerability of Sampling-Based Networks

To demonstrate the vulnerability of sampling-based CKKS network construction to overflow attacks, we deploy the attack described in Section 3 on classification NNs for tabular data (HELOC [30]), handwritten digit classification (MNIST [20]), and image classification (CIFAR [32]). We compare the vulnerability of a CKKS network constructed via sampled bounds to the vulnerability of an NN constructed with our approach. In both cases, we use GeLU\mathrm{GeLU} activation functions and heterogeneous polynomials. Table 1 provides an overview: Attacks are successful with non-zero probability on all NNs with sampled bounds. As expected, our approach is robust to the attacks.

Results.

For HELOC we generate sampled bounds using the first half of the dataset and use the other half for our attack. We allow perturbations of 15%15\% w.r.t. each feature’s range. To discretize values, our attack uses a straight-through-estimator [36]. We find three attacks on the sampled NN.

For MNIST we generate sampled bounds using the original MNIST dataset. Our attack is performed using the USPS dataset [37] (same input configuration and task setting). We allow rotations of up to 23∘23^{\circ}, translation by up to 20% and L∞L_{\infty}-noise of up to ε=5/255\varepsilon=5/255. We find our attack is successful in approx. 12.3% of cases and produces realistic inputs (see also Figure 9).

For CIFAR we generate sampled bounds using the original CIFAR dataset. We perform our attack using the independent CIFAR10.1 dataset [38, 39] (same input configuration and task setting). We allow rotations of 17∘17^{\circ} and L∞L_{\infty} noise of up to ε=15/255\varepsilon=15/255 (no translation due to non-black background in images). We find vulnerabilities in both the small and deep CIFAR NN. For the latter we find our attack succeeds on 46.7%46.7\% of images (see also Figure 11).

Reproduction in CKKS Circuit and Discussion.

Our attack initially only searches for perturbations that push the polynomial NN fπf_{\pi} outside its bounds. As discussed in Section 3, this overflow is likely to induce arithmetic errors on the CKKS circuit. Indeed, we validated our attack on a subset of MNIST attacks where we showed that all successful attacks on fπf_{\pi} lead to arithmetic errors in the CKKS circuit. This underscores the importance of eliminating overflows. As shown in Table 1, our certified design eliminates overflows without major impacts on the NN’s accuracy.

5.3 Certified Design at Scale

Here, we measure the verified error, cryptographic error, and predictive accuracy of our certified design. As per Section 5.1, we select GELU\gelu NNs, compute verified pre-activation bounds and fit multiple polynomials per layer.

The results in Table 2 show only very minor drops in classification accuracy (HELOC, MNIST, CIFAR), mean squared error (EC, RUL), or mean absolute error (NN4Sys). Although the verified bound on the approximation error |fπ​(x)−f​(x)||f_{\pi}(x)-f(x)| increases with network size, it is still fairly tight for most NNs – especially when compared to their typical output ranges. We also show the maximum CKKS error |fCKKS⊥​(x)−fπ​(x)||f^{\bot}_{\text{CKKS}}(x)-f_{\pi}(x)| obtained over a sample of the respective dataset.

More details about how the CKKS experiments have been performed are given in Appendix D. Additionally, as discussed in Section C, our design has a positive impact over the IND-CPAD{}^{\text{D}} security of the whole solution — which can be seen as a contribution of independent interest.

6 Conclusions and Directions for Future Work

In this paper, we demonstrate for the first time the vulnerability of current CKKS-based neural networks to overflow attacks. To solve this, we provide a framework to design certified neural networks. By construction, our approach yields networks that are provably overflow robust on the full input space, without sacrificing predictive performance.

Limitations and future work.

We see this work as a starting point for more robust FHE inference. Precise modelling of the CKKS noise like in [40, 41] could strengthen our bounds to include 𝒆CKKS{\bm{e}}_{\text{CKKS}}. Extending our certified design to arbitrary depth networks is possible in theory but requires the inclusion of bootstrapping and co-design of convolution layers [42] to reduce the CKKS noise. Finally, our method may occasionally generate polynomials with ill-scaled coefficients, which cause a reduction on the CKKS precision.
