Appendix A A general overview of FHE schemes

Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) is an advanced cryptographic primitive that, extending standard encryption, allows operations to be performed on encrypted data, without having access to the secret key. It was firstly theorized by Rivest, Adleman and Dertouzos in [43], and made possible by Gentry in its seminal work [44].

Some modern FHE schemes.

A few years after Gentry’s work, it is possible to find different approaches to build a FHE scheme from the (ring)-Learning with errors [45, 18] hard problem, and we can group them in two categories. The first performs very fast operations but on a single integer value at a time, has an easy programming model and lighter parameters. Originally introduced by Ducas and Micciancio in FHEW [46, 47], the reference scheme for this category is nowadays TFHE, introduced by Chillotti, Gama, Georgieva and Izabachène [6]. While TFHE allows one to compute arbitrary activation functions via (relatively small) lookup tables, it requires strong quantisation and lacks parallelism, which hampers its overall performance [48].

On the other hand, the second group includes schemes that allow operating on many values at the same time, following a single instruction, multiple data (SIMD) approach. The main reference schemes for this category are BGV/BFV [3, 4, 5] and CKKS [7]. The former operate on a plaintext space of the shape ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p} for some (modestly large) plaintext modulus p∈ℤ>0p\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}, and allow encoding many values in the same ciphertext [49] — thus enabling SIMD operations. We may refer to this category as exact-FHE. To see how the accumulated error can be removed during decryption, let us consider the case of BGV. There, a message m∈ℤpm\in\mathbb{Z}_{p} is encoded as m+p⋅em+p\cdot e for some small error term ee. Hence, by simply evaluating a modular reduction by pp, one can remove the final error. Unfortunately, this introduces a limit over the amount of values that can be encoded, namely values smaller than pp. Moreover, BGV and BFV are generally considered less suitable for deep FHE neural networks as they lack an efficient way to evaluate activation functions — only additions and multiplications in ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p} are available.

In contrast, CKKS [7], which we may call approximate-FHE, has as its plaintext space the complex space ℂ\mathbb{C}, and natively encodes vectors of complex numbers. It allows for approximate computations by considering the noise, naturally present for security reasons, as part of the message. Furthermore, it offers efficient primitives to compute vector operations such as element-wise additions, multiplications and rotations. For this reason, it is one of the preferred schemes for executing deep FHE neural networks [50].Currently, all the available FHE schemes are based on the hardness of the Ring-Learning With Errors (RLWE) problem [18], and, as every other lattice-based cryptography primitive, require injecting random noise during encryption process to ensure security.

Some fresh approaches.

Nowadays, we can find more exotic approaches to FHE, based on the classic schemes introduced in the previous paragraph. In particular, more recent schemes focus on improving the error growth in deep circuits and on the ability to represent large plaintext rings [51, 52, 53, 54, 55, 56]. In particular we refer the interested reader to, e.g., GBFV [53, 57], dBFV [58], discrete-CKKS [54, 55, 56], tuple-CKKS [52].

Appendix B The CKKS scheme

The Cheon-Kim-Kim-Song (CKKS) scheme, originally introduced in [7], currently represents the only framework to efficiently handle complex (and real) arithmetic in FHE55 5 An exception is given in [59], where the authors present an approach to handle float numbers in TFHE. That method, however, poorly fits neural network operations as it allows one to handle a single value at the time, while CKKS has a significant parallelization. As other FHE schemes, it is lattice-based and it has a security reduction to the hardness of the ring-Learning with Errors (RLWE) problem [18]. This is a structured version of the original Learning with errors (LWE) introduced for efficiency reasons.

Definition B.1 (Ring learning with errors (RLWE) [18]).

Let χs,χe\chi_{s},\chi_{e} be distributions over ℛ:=ℤ⁡[X]/(XN+1)\mathcal{R}:=\mathbb{Z}[X]/(X^{N}+1). The goal of the RLWE problem is to distinguish (𝒂,𝒙)({\bm{a}},{\bm{x}}) from (𝒂,𝒂​𝒔+𝒆)({\bm{a}},{\bm{a}}{\bm{s}}+{\bm{e}}) for uniformly random 𝒂,𝒙∈ℛQ{\bm{a}},{\bm{x}}\in\mathcal{R}_{Q}, 𝒆←χ𝒆{\bm{e}}\leftarrow\chi_{\bm{e}}, and 𝒔←χ𝒔{\bm{s}}\leftarrow\chi_{\bm{s}}. The RLWEN,Q,χe,χe{}_{N,Q,\chi_{e},\chi_{e}} assumption is that solving the RLWEN,Q,χe,χe{}_{N,Q,\chi_{e},\chi_{e}} problem is unfeasible.

In this work, we employ an optimized version of the CKKS scheme which uses the double Chinese Remainder Theorem (DCRT) representation of polynomials [60], implemented in the OpenFHE library [17].

Basics of CKKS.

Let N=2kN=2^{k} for some integer k>0k>0 and Q>0Q>0 being some large modulus. Let DFT:ℝ⁡[X]/(XN+1)→ℂN/2\text{DFT}:\mathbb{R}[X]/(X^{N}+1)\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{N/2} be a discrete Fourier transform (DFT) defined as 𝒎⁡(X)↦(𝒎⁡(ζ5i))0≤i<N/2{\bm{m}}(X)\mapsto({\bm{m}}(\zeta^{5^{i}}))_{0\leq i<N/2}, and let iDFT:ℂN/2→ℝ⁡[X]/(XN+1)\text{iDFT}:\mathbb{C}^{N/2}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}[X]/(X^{N}+1) be its inverse, with ζ\zeta being a 2​N2N-th primitive root of unity. The cleartext space of CKKS is ℂN/2\mathbb{C}^{N/2}, the plaintext space (i.e., after the encoding) is ℛ:=ℤ⁡[X]/(XN+1)\mathcal{R}:=\mathbb{Z}[X]/(X^{N}+1), and the ciphertext space is ℛQ2\mathcal{R}_{Q}^{2}. In order to make the cleartext space compatible with RLWE encryption (which takes a message in ℛ\mathcal{R}, and returns a ciphertext in ℛq2\mathcal{R}_{q}^{2}), the CKKS scheme uses (the inverse of) a discrete Fourier transform encoding that moves a plaintext from ℂN/2\mathbb{C}^{N/2} to ℛ\mathcal{R} as follows:

ℂN/2⏟Cleartext→iDFTℝ⁡[X]/(XN+1)⏟Plaintext→Roundingℤ⁡[X]/(XN+1)⏟Plaintext→EncryptionℛQ2⏟Ciphertext,\underbrace{\mathbb{C}^{N/2}}_{\text{Cleartext}}\xrightarrow{\;\;\;\text{iDFT}\;\;\;}\underbrace{\mathbb{R}[X]/(X^{N}+1)}_{\text{Plaintext}}\xrightarrow{\;\;\;\text{Rounding}\;\;\;}\underbrace{\mathbb{Z}[X]/(X^{N}+1)}_{\text{Plaintext}}\xrightarrow{\;\;\;\text{Encryption}\;\;\;}\underbrace{\mathcal{R}_{Q}^{2}}_{\text{Ciphertext}},

where the rounding follows ideas from [18, Section 2]. As it will be shown later, this rounding operation implies that we are required to scale the message by some large factor Δ>0\Delta>0 to preserve the most significant digits. In practice, numbers behave similarly to a fixed-point system, where precision is uniform across all values regardless of their size. The scaling factor Δ\Delta is the key parameter governing computational precision: increasing it yields greater accuracy but comes at the cost of (i) making computations more expensive and (ii) requiring a larger modulus QQ — which impacts the security.

Additionally, given the homomorphisms induced by the (i)DFT:

a+b=DFT⁡(iDFT⁡(a)+iDFT⁡(b))anda⊙b=DFT⁡(iDFT⁡(a)⋅iDFT⁡(b)),\begin{split}a+b=\mathrm{DFT}(\mathrm{iDFT}(a)+\mathrm{iDFT}(b))\quad\text{and}\quad a\odot b=\mathrm{DFT}(\mathrm{iDFT}(a)\cdot\mathrm{iDFT}(b)),\end{split}

where ⊙\odot is the slot-wise multiplication, this naturally induces a SIMD computational paradigm on the plaintext space by simply multiplying ciphertexts in the iDFT domain.

We can summarize the main operations of the scheme as follows.

  • •

    CKKS.Setup(1λ,N,L)(1^{\lambda},N,L). Given a security parameter λ\lambda, a ring dimension NN, and a multiplicative circuit depth LL, choose a modulus chain Q=∏i=1ℓqiQ=\prod_{i=1}^{\ell}q_{i}, a secret key distribution χs\chi_{s}, an error distribution χe\chi_{e}, and a scaling factor Δ∈ℤ>0\Delta\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}. Output the public parameter tuple

    𝒕:=(N,Δ,Q,χs,χe).{\bm{t}}:=\bigl(N,\;\Delta,\;Q,\;\chi_{s},\;\chi_{e}\bigr).
  • •

    CKKS.Keygen(𝒕)({\bm{t}}). Given the public parameter tuple 𝐭\mathbf{t}, sample 𝒔∼χs{\bm{s}}\sim\chi_{s} from ℛ\mathcal{R}, 𝐚←ℛQL\mathbf{a}\leftarrow\mathcal{R}_{Q_{L}} uniformly, and 𝐞∼χe\mathbf{e}\sim\chi_{e}. Output the secret and public keys

    sk:=𝒔,pk:=(−𝒂⋅𝒔+𝒆,𝒂)=:(pk0,pk1)∈ℛQL2.sk:={\bm{s}},\qquad pk:=\bigl(-{\bm{a}}\cdot{\bm{s}}+{\bm{e}},\;{\bm{a}}\bigr)=:(pk_{0},pk_{1})\;\in\;\mathcal{R}_{Q_{L}}^{2}.

    Note that p​k0+p​k1⋅𝒔=𝒆≈0pk_{0}+pk_{1}\cdot{\bm{s}}={\bm{e}}\approx 0, so the public key is a noisy encryption of zero under 𝒔{\bm{s}}.

  • •

    CKKS.Encode(𝐦)(\mathbf{m}). Given a cleartext vector 𝐦∈ℂN/2\mathbf{m}\in\mathbb{C}^{N/2}, apply an inverse DFT and scale by Δ\Delta. Output the plaintext ring element

    ⌊Δ⋅𝗂𝖣𝖥𝖳⁡(𝒎)⌉∈ℛ.\bigl\lfloor\Delta\cdot\mathsf{iDFT}({\bm{m}})\bigr\rceil\;\in\;\mathcal{R}.
  • •

    CKKS.Decode(𝒑)({\bm{p}}). Given a plaintext 𝒑∈ℛ{\bm{p}}\in\mathcal{R}, apply a DFT and rescale by 1/Δ1/\Delta. Output the approximate cleartext vector

    1Δ⋅𝖣𝖥𝖳⁡(𝒑)∈ℂN/2.\frac{1}{\Delta}\cdot\mathsf{DFT}({\bm{p}})\;\in\;\mathbb{C}^{N/2}.
  • •

    CKKS.Encrypt(𝒑)({\bm{p}}). Given a plaintext 𝒑∈ℛQL{\bm{p}}\in\mathcal{R}_{Q_{L}} and the public key p​kpk, sample an ephemeral mask 𝒖∼χs{\bm{u}}\sim\chi_{s} and noise terms 𝒆0,𝒆1∼χe{\bm{e}}_{0},{\bm{e}}_{1}\sim\chi_{e}. Output the ciphertext

    ([p​k0​𝒖+𝒆0+𝐩]QL,[p​k1​𝒖+𝒆1]QL)∈ℛQL2.\bigl([pk_{0}\,{\bm{u}}+{\bm{e}}_{0}+\mathbf{p}]_{Q_{L}},\;[pk_{1}\,{\bm{u}}+{\bm{e}}_{1}]_{Q_{L}}\bigr)\;\in\;\mathcal{R}_{Q_{L}}^{2}.
  • •

    CKKS.Decrypt(𝒄)({\bm{c}}). Given a ciphertext 𝒄=(c0,c1)∈ℛQL2{\bm{c}}=(c_{0},c_{1})\in\mathcal{R}_{Q_{L}}^{2} and the secret key 𝒔{\bm{s}}, compute the inner product c0+c1​𝐬c_{0}+c_{1}\,\mathbf{s}. Output the approximate plaintext

    c0+c1​𝐬=(p​k0​𝒖+𝒆0+𝒑)+(p​k1​𝒖+𝒆1)​𝒔=(−𝒂​𝒔+𝒆)​𝒖+𝒆0+𝒑+𝒂​𝒖​𝒔+𝒆1​𝒔=𝒆⋅𝒖+𝒆0+𝒆1​𝒔⏟small noise+𝒑≈𝒑∈ℛQL.\begin{split}c_{0}+c_{1}\,\mathbf{s}&=\bigl(pk_{0}\,{\bm{u}}+{\bm{e}}_{0}+{\bm{p}}\bigr)+\bigl(pk_{1}\,{\bm{u}}+{\bm{e}}_{1}\bigr){\bm{s}}\\ &=\bigl(-{\bm{a}}{\bm{s}}+{\bm{e}}\bigr){\bm{u}}+{\bm{e}}_{0}+{\bm{p}}+{\bm{a}}\,{\bm{u}}\,{\bm{s}}+{\bm{e}}_{1}\,{\bm{s}}\\ &=\underbrace{{\bm{e}}\cdot{\bm{u}}+{\bm{e}}_{0}+{\bm{e}}_{1}\,{\bm{s}}}_{\text{small noise}}+{\bm{p}}\;\approx\;{\bm{p}}\;\in\;\mathcal{R}_{Q_{L}}.\end{split}

Encryption and decryption follow from standard RLWE encryption [18]. Notice that the CKKS noise is given by two factors: the rounding performed in the encoding and the error inject during encryption.

Homomorphic operations.

The CKKS scheme enables different homomorphic operations, we report in the following some of them:

  • •

    CKKS.Add(𝒄,𝒄′)({\bm{c}},{\bm{c}}^{\prime}). Given two ciphertexts 𝒄,𝒄′∈ℛQℓ2{\bm{c}},{\bm{c}}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}_{Q_{\ell}}^{2}, output the component-wise sum

    𝒄add:=𝒄+𝒄′=(c0+c0′,c1+c1′)∈ℛQℓ2,{\bm{c}}_{\text{add}}\;:=\;{\bm{c}}+{\bm{c}}^{\prime}\;=\;(c_{0}+c_{0}^{\prime},\;c_{1}+c_{1}^{\prime})\;\in\;\mathcal{R}_{Q_{\ell}}^{2},

    which satisfies Decrypt​(𝒄add)≈Decrypt​(𝒄)+Decrypt​(𝒄′)\text{Decrypt}({\bm{c}}_{\text{add}})\approx\text{Decrypt}({\bm{c}})+\text{Decrypt}({\bm{c}}^{\prime}).

  • •

    CKKS.Mul(𝒄,𝒄′)({\bm{c}},{\bm{c}}^{\prime}). Given two ciphertexts 𝒄,𝒄′∈ℛQℓ2{\bm{c}},{\bm{c}}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}_{Q_{\ell}}^{2}, compute the degree-2 tensor product

    (c0​c0′,c0​c1′+c1​c0′,c1​c1′)∈ℛQℓ3,(c_{0}c_{0}^{\prime},\;c_{0}c_{1}^{\prime}+c_{1}c_{0}^{\prime},\;c_{1}c_{1}^{\prime})\;\in\;\mathcal{R}_{Q_{\ell}}^{3},

    and apply KeySwitch(⋅,sk2→sk)\text{KeySwitch}(\,\cdot\,,sk^{2}\to sk) to reduce back to two components. Output

    𝒄mul∈ℛQℓ2,{\bm{c}}_{\text{mul}}\;\in\;\mathcal{R}_{Q_{\ell}}^{2},

    which satisfies Decrypt​(𝒄mul)≈Decrypt​(𝒄)⋅Decrypt​(𝒄′)\text{Decrypt}({\bm{c}}_{\text{mul}})\approx\text{Decrypt}({\bm{c}})\cdot\text{Decrypt}({\bm{c}}^{\prime}). Note that the resulting scaling factor is Δ2\Delta^{2}; a subsequent call to Rescale is typically needed to restore it to Δ\Delta.

  • •

    CKKS.KeySwitch(𝒄,e​v​k)({\bm{c}},evk). Given a ciphertext 𝒄=(c0,c1,c2)∈ℛQℓ3{\bm{c}}=(c_{0},c_{1},c_{2})\in\mathcal{R}_{Q_{\ell}}^{3} encrypted under s​k2sk^{2} and an evaluation key e​v​kevk — a public encryption of s​k2sk^{2} under s​ksk — decompose c2c_{2} into a base-PP representation c2=∑jc2(j)​Pjc_{2}=\sum_{j}c_{2}^{(j)}P^{j} and absorb it into the first two components using e​v​kevk. Output the key-switched ciphertext

    (c0+∑jc2(j)​e​v​k0(j),c1+∑jc2(j)​e​v​k1(j))∈ℛQℓ2,\bigl(c_{0}+\textstyle\sum_{j}c_{2}^{(j)}\,evk_{0}^{(j)},\;c_{1}+\textstyle\sum_{j}c_{2}^{(j)}\,evk_{1}^{(j)}\bigr)\;\in\;\mathcal{R}_{Q_{\ell}}^{2},

    which encrypts the same plaintext under s​ksk with a controlled increase in noise.

  • •

    CKKS.Rescale(𝒄)({\bm{c}}). Given a ciphertext 𝒄∈ℛQℓ2{\bm{c}}\in\mathcal{R}_{Q_{\ell}}^{2} with scaling factor Δ2\Delta^{2}, drop the last modulus qℓq_{\ell} from the chain and divide. Output

    ⌊Δ−1⋅𝒄⌉∈ℛQℓ−12,\bigl\lfloor\Delta^{-1}\cdot{\bm{c}}\bigr\rceil\;\in\;\mathcal{R}_{Q_{\ell-1}}^{2},

    which restores the scaling factor to Δ\Delta at the cost of consuming one level of the modulus chain.

  • •

    CKKS.Rotate(𝒄,i)({\bm{c}},i). Given a ciphertext 𝒄∈ℛQℓ2{\bm{c}}\in\mathcal{R}_{Q_{\ell}}^{2} and a rotation index i∈ℤi\in\mathbb{Z}, apply the Galois automorphism σi:X↦X5imod2​N\sigma_{i}\colon X\mapsto X^{5^{i}\bmod 2N} component-wise to obtain σi​(𝒄)∈ℛQℓ2\sigma_{i}({\bm{c}})\in\mathcal{R}_{Q_{\ell}}^{2}, and apply KeySwitch(⋅,σi(sk)→sk)\text{KeySwitch}(\,\cdot\,,\sigma_{i}(sk)\to sk) using the corresponding rotation key. Output

    𝒄rot∈ℛQℓ2,{\bm{c}}_{\text{rot}}\;\in\;\mathcal{R}_{Q_{\ell}}^{2},

    which satisfies Decrypt​(𝒄rot)≈ρi​(Decrypt​(𝒄))\text{Decrypt}({\bm{c}}_{\text{rot}})\approx\rho^{i}\!\left(\text{Decrypt}({\bm{c}})\right), where ρi\rho^{i} denotes a cyclic shift of the plaintext slot vector by ii positions.

Appendix C About the security of CKKS–based machine learning.

Remark that, in the (approximate) CKKS scheme, the encrypted message 𝒎∈ℂN/2{\bm{m}}\in\mathbb{C}^{N/2} is added with some noise 𝒆ckks∈ℂN/2{\bm{e}}_{\text{ckks}}\in\mathbb{C}^{N/2} for security reasons. One peculiar point of CKKS is that the encrypted message is 𝒎+𝒆ckks{\bm{m}}+{\bm{e}}_{\text{ckks}}, and the error can not be separated from the message66 6 For the sake of completeness, there are cases, e.g., discrete-CKKS [61], where the error can be removed. This implies an assumption over the plaintext space of CKKS, from ℂ\mathbb{C} to some discrete set of it, e.g., {0,1}\{0,1\}. Note that discrete-CKKS is typically not employed for privacy–preserving machine learning. Li and Micciancio showed [62] that an adversary with access to the decryption error of a CKKS ciphertext through a decryption oracle can mount passive key-recovery attack. Such attack is captured by the so-called IND-CPAD{}^{\text{D}} model [62, Def. 2], and all countermeasures known to date require the user to compute a bound on the decryption error.

The threat model in this setting as follows: an attacker can have access to decryptions of CKKS ciphertexts — which in real world scenarios can be a very common setup — and she wants to recover information about the secret key. The attacker then asks for a decryption of zero, thus obtaining 𝒆ckks{\bm{e}}_{\text{ckks}}. Remark that decryption is performed as [⟨s​k,c⟩]q[\langle sk,c\rangle]_{q}, so the noise directly depends on s​ksk, and this can be exploited to mount a key–recovery attack. We refer to [62, 63] for further info.

We believe that this work can serve as an improvement in terms of security with respect to the IND-CPAD{}^{\text{D}} model. In fact, the strongest countermeasures require the final CKKS error to be bounded to apply some procedure before decryption (e.g., converting the results to discrete-CKKS [61], noise flooding, and so on). In particular, our work allows one to precisely identify the CKKS error as follows. Typical neural networks based on CKKS output the result in the form

𝒎+𝒆ckks+𝒆approx,{\bm{m}}+{\bm{e}}_{\text{ckks}}+{\bm{e}}_{\text{approx}},

where 𝒆ckks{\bm{e}}_{\text{ckks}} is the CKKS error and 𝒆approx{\bm{e}}_{\text{approx}} is the error naturally introduced by the fact that polynomial approximations of the activation functions are used. Note that 𝒆approx{\bm{e}}_{\text{approx}} is defined with respect to the result of the plain version of the network. On the other hand, our output will be in the form

𝒎+𝒆ckks,{\bm{m}}+{\bm{e}}_{\text{ckks}},

as we implement exactly the same network in the plain and in the encrypted worlds (i.e., we do not perform approximations in the encrypted domain). Therefore, our result will not be corrupted by 𝒆approx{\bm{e}}_{\text{approx}}. For instance, one could combine our work with [41], to have a strong theoretical foundation on error growth during the evaluation of the circuit; namely it is possible to define somewhat tight bounds on 𝒆ckks{\bm{e}}_{\text{ckks}} and to take countermeasures.

On the other hand, bounding 𝒆approx{\bm{e}}_{\text{approx}} is much harder task and implies very large bounds, especially in deep networks. We are not aware of any previous work that allows one to identify with a good precision the CKKS error in a neural network output.

On the role of error in standard CKKS neural networks vs in our work

It is very common to observe performance degradation (e.g., accuracy) in CKKS–based neural networks [20, 64, 65, 66]. In practice, this means that the performance of the plain and the encrypted networks do not coincide. This is usually tackled by using larger degrees for the polynomials approximating the activation functions, although it can quickly become unpractical — especially for deep circuits.

On the other hand, since our networks are constructed natively using polynomials, the output logits contain no approximation error in the classical sense, but will only contain the CKKS error. Notice that we can immediately identify the CKKS error as L∞​(𝒚−𝒚CKKS)L_{\infty}({\bm{y}}-{\bm{y}}_{\text{CKKS}}). As discussed above, it is possible to reduce it simply by increasing the values of qiq_{i} and Δ\Delta. This is not possible in other works as it gets mixed with the polynomial approximation error, meaning that, by using our solution, improving the precision of the result is as natural as increasing the magnitude of the two parameters that control the fixed-point accuracy of CKKS.

Appendix D From a certified network to a CKKS program

As an additional contribution, to evaluate our encrypted circuits, we designed a compiler that, given a network (defined as a list of layers), generates a JSON file that follows the grammar defined in Figure 6.

In particular, our OpenFHE implementation takes as input a JSON file containing the network definition and automatically evaluates the network. In practice, we implemented methods to evaluate the ⟨linear-layer⟩\langle\text{linear-layer}\rangle and ⟨chebyshev-layer⟩\langle\text{chebyshev-layer}\rangle tuples automatically77 7 For convolutions, we used ad-hoc source codes as their evaluation is harder to automate. However, our framework is flexible enough to allow for the automatic evaluation of convolutions by simply defining a function that handles the ⟨conv-layer⟩\langle\text{conv-layer}\rangle tuple.

Automatic evaluation of linear layers.

We implemented simple algorithms to evaluate linear layers. We first define the following encodings.

Definition D.1 (Repeated encoding).

Given a vector 𝒗∈ℝn{\bm{v}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, its repeated encoding is a vector 𝒗′∈ℝn2{\bm{v}}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{n^{2}} where 𝒗{\bm{v}} is repeated nn times. Visually:

𝒗′:=(v1,v2,…,vn|v1,v2,…,vn|…)∈ℝn2.{\bm{v}}^{\prime}:=(v_{1},v_{2},\dots,v_{n}\,|\,v_{1},v_{2},\dots,v_{n}\,|\,\dots)\in\mathbb{R}^{n^{2}}.
Definition D.2 (Expanded encoding).

Given a vector 𝒗∈ℝn{\bm{v}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, its expanded encoding is a vector 𝒗′∈ℝn2{\bm{v}}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{n^{2}} where each component viv_{i} of 𝒗{\bm{v}} is repeated nn times. Visually:

𝒗′:=(v1,v1,…,v1|v2,v2,…,v2|…)∈ℝn2.{\bm{v}}^{\prime}:=(v_{1},v_{1},\dots,v_{1}\,|\,v_{2},v_{2},\dots,v_{2}\,|\,\dots)\in\mathbb{R}^{n^{2}}.

We use two different input encodings as we employ two different algorithms to evaluate the typical W​𝒙+𝒃W{\bm{x}}+{\bm{b}} transformation, depending on how the input is encoded (Algorithm 1 and 2).

Automatic evaluation of Chebyshev layers.

The evaluation of Chebyshev polynomials follows the footprint firsly introduced in [16] — which in turn implements a version of the Paterson-Stockmeyer algorithm [15] adapted for Chebyshev bases — however our approach is slightly more general as in [16] they assume to evaluate a single polynomial in all the slots of a ciphertext. On the other hand, in our construction we require to evaluate a different polynomial for each slot. Luckily, we can use the strategy described in [16, Section 3.1] and replace the usage of constants coefficents cic_{i} to packed coefficients in a plaintext as 𝒄i{\bm{c}}_{i}. The following corollary easily follows.

Corollary D.1 (generalizes [16, Theorem 1]).

There exists an algorithm in CKKS to evaluate dd polynomials of degree nn given in Chebyshev base with 2​n+O⁡(log⁡(n))\sqrt{2n}+O(\log(n)) non-scalar multiplications and O⁡(n)O(n) scalar multiplications, with dd being the number of available slots in a CKKS ciphertext.

We remark that the cost of evaluating a single polynomial in all slots or a different polynomial, one for each slot, is the same as constants are typically encoded in plaintexts in order to be compatible with the CKKS multiplication88 8 Minor differences might occur in practice depending on how the multiplication algorithms are implemented for constants vs. plaintexts, but we ignore them. We therefore used such algorithm to allow for the evaluation of different polynomials in different slots. Since the original OpenFHE implementation of CKKS does not provide such an algorithm, we used a custom fork that enables the usage of the EvalChebyshevSeriesPSBatch.

Automatic parameters selection.

Given a JSON network, the program adapts the choice of the underlying CKKS scheme by first computing the required multiplicative depth. In practice, Algorithm 1 requires 1 multiplications and Algorithm 2 requires 2. On the other hand, the depth required by the evaluation of Chebyshev polynomials (Corollary D.1) depends on the degree as shown in Table 3.

We designed our software in such a way that the FHE parameters are automatically chosen to support the minimum multiplicative depth required by the network and at the same time to support λ>128\lambda>128 bits of (classical) security according to [67]. We present the sets of parameters, one for each network, in Table 4.

We remark that NN controls the size of the ring ℤ⁡[X]/(XN+1)\mathbb{Z}[X]/(X^{N}+1), and as a side effects it also controls the maximum amount of values that can be encoded into a ciphertext (i.e., a power of two ≤N/2\leq N/2 due to the DFT encoding, see Appendix B). On the other hand, the modulus Q=∏i=1ℓqiQ=\prod_{i=1}^{\ell}q_{i} controls the maximum amount of multiplications, followed by a rescaling, that can be performed over a ciphertext, namely ℓ−1\ell-1. In practice, the final modulus is defined as Q​PQP, where PP is an additional modulus required to reduce the amount of error introduced by multiplications (refer to [68]). In turn, the magnitude of PP depends on dnumd_{\text{num}}: larger values correspond to smaller moduli PP.

We refer the interested reader to [60] — which describes the actual CKKS implementation used in our work — for an extensive discussion about the impact of each parameter.

On the IND-CPA security of our solution.

We use CKKS in leveled mode and do not resort to bootstrapping [19]. This allows us to use a more conservative choice in terms of secret key, we will indeed use a uniform ternary distribution, where entries are chosen uniformly at random from {−1,0,1}\{-1,0,1\}. This means that, in practice, in order to obtain λ>128\lambda>128 bits of security, for N=216N=2^{16} we require Q​P<21747QP<2^{1747} and for N=217N=2^{17}, Q​P<23523QP<2^{3523} (refer to [67, Table 5.2]).

Appendix E Additional Background on Polynomial Approximation and Smoothness

Section 4.3 showed that the polynomial approximation error for a fixed approximation interval converges significantly faster, the smoother the function is. The bounds presented in Equation (4) and Equation (5) used the concepts of total variation and Bernstein ellipses, for which we provide background in Subsections E.1 and E.2, respectively.

Additionally, we show in Figure 7(a), how increases in width of the approximation interval affect the precision of polynomial approximations of fixed degree - both for the ReLU\relu and the GELU\gelu function. We can see that for smaller radii rr of the approximation interval [−r,r][-r,r], the GELU\gelu approximation is much better than ReLU\relu. However, as the radius increases, quality of the approximations becomes similar. The Figure further illustrates, the benefits of fitting polynomial approximations using the Remez algorithm [22] as opposed to standard Chebyshev interpolation. High-quality polynomial approximations computed by the Remez algorithm are roughly twice as precise as Chebyshev approximations.

E.1 Total Variation

For a more extensive treatment of total variation, we refer the reader to Appell et al. [69]. Let f:ℝ→ℝf:\R\to\R be a function and τ\tau a partition of the interval [l,u][l,u] into mm subintervals with boundary points t0=l<t1<t2<…<tm=ut_{0}=l<t_{1}<t_{2}<...<t_{m}=u. Then the total variation of ff over the interval [l,u][l,u]

V[l,u]​(f)=supτ∑i=0m−1|f⁡(ti+1)−f⁡(ti)|\displaystyle V_{[l,u]}(f)=\sup_{\tau}\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}|f(t_{i+1})-f(t_{i})| (7)

is defined as the supremum of the above sum over all possible partitions. If V[l,u]​(f)<∞V_{[l,u]}(f)<\infty, then ff is of bounded total variation over [l,u][l,u].

In some cases, there are easier formulas to compute total variation. If ff is monotonic over [l,u][l,u], then ff is of bounded total variation over [l,u][l,u] and

V[l,u]​(f)=|f⁡(u)−f⁡(l)|.\displaystyle V_{[l,u]}(f)=|f(u)-f(l)|\;. (8)

If ff is continuously differentiable over [l,u][l,u], then

V[l,u]​(f)=∫lu|f′​(x)|​𝑑x.\displaystyle V_{[l,u]}(f)=\int_{l}^{u}|f^{\prime}(x)|\;dx\;. (9)

E.2 Bernstein Ellipse

The further a function ff can be continued into the complex plane, the faster the rate of convergence for the polynomial approximation error. The bound given in Equation (5) uses the largest parameter ρ\rho, s.t. ff can be analytically continued to the interior of the Bernstein ellipse

Eρ={z∈ℂ|z=u+u−12,u=ρei​θ,ρ≥1,0≤θ<2π}\displaystyle E_{\rho}=\left\{z\in\mathbb{C}~\middle|~z=\frac{u+u^{-1}}{2},~~u=\rho e^{i\theta},~~\rho\geq 1,~~0\leq\theta<2\pi\right\} (10)

as a measurement for how far into the complex plane ff can be extended (definition of EρE_{\rho} taken from Wang et al. [70]). Bernstein ellipses for varius choices of ρ\rho are illustrated in Figure 7(b).

If ff is entire (i.e. it can be analytically continued to all ℂ\mathbb{C}), then, one can choose any parameter ρ\rho for the Bernstein ellipse that leads to a favourable value of M=maxx∈Eρ⁡|f⁡(x)|M=\max_{x\in E_{\rho}}|f(x)| in Equation (5).

Appendix F Improved GELU Relaxation

In an attempt to compute tighter bounds for Equation (2) for the GELU\gelu activation, we tried to improve upon the parameterized GELU\gelu relaxation given by Shi et al. [71] used in α\alpha-CROWN [24]. While our relaxation achieves bounds that are significantly tighter at parameter initialization, the difference to the relaxation by Shi et al. after parameter optimization is minimal. Since we used our relaxation in our code, we nevertheless give a brief overview over its construction.

At a high level, we provide linear over- and underapproximations

a¯​(α1,l,u)​x+b¯​(α1,l,u)≤GELU⁡(x)≤a¯​(α2,α3,l,u)+b¯​(α2,α3,l,u)∀x∈[l,u],\displaystyle\underline{a}(\alpha_{1},l,u)x+\underline{b}(\alpha_{1},l,u)\leq\gelu(x)\leq\overline{a}(\alpha_{2},\alpha_{3},l,u)+\overline{b}(\alpha_{2},\alpha_{3},l,u)\quad\forall x\in[l,u]\;, (11)

where our relaxation is parameterized by a lower tangent point α1\alpha_{1}, an upper left tangent point α2\alpha_{2} and an upper right tangent point α3\alpha_{3}. We then use the case distinction shown in Figure 8 to select if one of the tangents or a secant line is a valid lower or upper bound.

The GELU\gelu function is concave for x∈(−∞,−2]x\in(-\infty,-\sqrt{2}] and x∈[2,∞)x\in[\sqrt{2},\infty). This relates to the cases concave left and concave right in Figure 8. If [l,u][l,u] is completely within these regions, the secant is always the best linear lower bound and the tangent at any point x∈[l,u]x\in[l,u] is a valid linear upper bound. For initialization, we set the tangent point (either α2\alpha_{2} or α3\alpha_{3}) to t=1/2⋅(l+u)t=1/2\cdot(l+u). This choice leads to an area-optimal overapproximation [72].

Since GELU\gelu is convex for x∈[−2,2]x\in[-\sqrt{2},\sqrt{2}], we can use the secant as an upper bound and set α1\alpha_{1} similarly as above.

In the cases non-convex middle increasing and outer, we can use the secant as a valid upper bound and the tangent at t∈[l′,u′]t\in[l^{\prime},u^{\prime}] for some l≤l′,u′≤ul\leq l^{\prime},u^{\prime}\leq u as a valid lower bound. We employ the same procedure as Shi et al. [71] for finding l′,u′l^{\prime},u^{\prime} and clamp the value of α1\alpha_{1} to these bounds if necessary.

For the cases middle decreasing II and non-convex positive II, the secant is a valid lower bound and the tangent at t∈[l,u′]t\in[l,u^{\prime}], respectively the tangent at t∈[l′,u]t\in[l^{\prime},u] is a valid upper bound. In these cases, we initialize α2\alpha_{2} or α3\alpha_{3} by computing 1/2⋅(l+u)1/2\cdot(l+u) and clamping to the valid bounds.

Finally, for middle decreasing I and non-convex positive I, the tangent at t∈[l′,u′]t\in[l^{\prime},u^{\prime}] is a valid lower bound and the tangent at t∈[l,u′′]t\in[l,u^{\prime\prime}] or respectively t∈[l′′,u]t\in[l^{\prime\prime},u] is a valid upper bound. As initialization for α1,α2\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2} and α3\alpha_{3}, we choose again the mid-point of the interval [l,u][l,u] clamped to the valid tangent point ranges.

Appendix G Additional Information on Differential Verification for Neural Networks

In this section, we provide information for how to instantiate the differential relaxation presented in Theorem 4.2 for the GELU\gelu function and report an optimization used to tighten the verified differential bounds.

But first, we provide helpful derivations for expressing differences at the current layer by differences in the preceding layer.

G.1 Additional Derivations

As stated in Section 4.4, approaches for differential verification of neural networks [27, 28, 29, 23] use that neuron-wise differences between networks 𝒩1\net_{1} and 𝒩2\net_{2} can be expressed in terms of the neuron-wise differences of previous layers. In this section, we give a brief derivation of these expressions.

The difference 𝚫~(l)=𝐲~1(l)−𝐲~2(l)\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mathbf{\Delta}}}^{(l)}=\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}}_{1}^{(l)}-\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}}_{2}^{(l)} between two pre-activation values can be partially expressed in terms of the difference 𝚫(l−1)=𝐲1(l−1)−𝐲2(l−1)\boldsymbol{\mathbf{\Delta}}^{(l-1)}=\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}_{1}^{(l-1)}-\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}_{2}^{(l-1)} between the post activation values of the previous layer as

𝚫~(l)\displaystyle\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mathbf{\Delta}}}^{(l)} =𝐲~1−𝐲~2=(W1​𝐲1(l−1)+𝐛1)−(W2​𝐲2(l−1)+𝐛2)\displaystyle=\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}}_{1}-\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}}_{2}=\left(W_{1}\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}_{1}^{(l-1)}+\boldsymbol{\mathbf{b}}_{1}\right)-\left(W_{2}\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}_{2}^{(l-1)}+\boldsymbol{\mathbf{b}}_{2}\right) (12)
=(W1​(𝐲1(l−1)−𝐲2(l−1))+𝐲2(l−1)+𝐛1)−(W2​𝐲2(l−1)+𝐛2)\displaystyle=\left(W_{1}\left(\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}_{1}^{(l-1)}-\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}_{2}^{(l-1)}\right)+\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}_{2}^{(l-1)}+\boldsymbol{\mathbf{b}}_{1}\right)-\left(W_{2}\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}_{2}^{(l-1)}+\boldsymbol{\mathbf{b}}_{2}\right) (13)
=(W1−W2)​𝐲2(l−1)+W1​(𝐲1(l−1)−𝐲2(l−1))+(𝐛1−𝐛2)\displaystyle=\left(W_{1}-W_{2}\right)\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}_{2}^{(l-1)}+W_{1}\left(\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}_{1}^{(l-1)}-\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}_{2}^{(l-1)}\right)+\left(\boldsymbol{\mathbf{b}}_{1}-\boldsymbol{\mathbf{b}}_{2}\right) (14)
=(W1−W2)​𝐲2(l−1)+W1​𝚫(l−1)+(𝐛1−𝐛2).\displaystyle=\left(W_{1}-W_{2}\right)\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}_{2}^{(l-1)}+W_{1}\boldsymbol{\mathbf{\Delta}}^{(l-1)}+\left(\boldsymbol{\mathbf{b}}_{1}-\boldsymbol{\mathbf{b}}_{2}\right)\;. (15)

Rewriting the difference to partially depend on 𝐲1(l−1)\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}_{1}^{(l-1)} is also possible.

A similar relation can be derived for the difference between activation values 𝚫(l)=𝐲1(l)−𝐲2(l)\boldsymbol{\mathbf{\Delta}}^{(l)}=\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}_{1}^{(l)}-\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}_{2}^{(l)} using

𝚫(l)\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\mathbf{\Delta}}^{(l)} =𝐲1(l)−𝐲2(l)=f⁡(𝐲~1(l))−g⁡(𝐲~2(l))\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}_{1}^{(l)}-\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}_{2}^{(l)}=f\left(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}}_{1}^{(l)}\right)-g\left(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}}_{2}^{(l)}\right) (16)
=f⁡(𝐲~1(l))−g⁡(𝐲~1(l)−(𝐲~1(l)−𝐲~2(l)))=f⁡(𝐲~1(l))−g⁡(𝐲~1(l)−𝚫~(l)).\displaystyle=f\left(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}}_{1}^{(l)}\right)-g\left(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}}_{1}^{(l)}-\left(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}}_{1}^{(l)}-\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}}_{2}^{(l)}\right)\right)=f\left(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}}_{1}^{(l)}\right)-g\left(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}}_{1}^{(l)}-\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mathbf{\Delta}}}^{(l)}\right)\;. (17)

G.2 Bounds on the Derivative of GELU\gelu

Instantiating the differential relaxation for p⁡(x)−σ⁡(x−Δ)p(x)-\sigma(x-\Delta) as described in Theorem 4.2 for σ=GELU\sigma=\gelu, requires computing bounds on the derivative GELU′⁡(x)\gelu^{\prime}(x) of the GELU\gelu function over an interval x∈[l,u]x\in[l,u].

Since GELU⁡(x)\gelu(x) is concave for D1=(−∞,−2]D_{1}=(-\infty,-\sqrt{2}], convex for D2=[−2,2]D_{2}=[-\sqrt{2},\sqrt{2}] and concave for D3=[2,∞)D_{3}=[\sqrt{2},\infty), its derivative is monotonically decreasing, monotonically increasing and monotonically decreasing over the respective domains. Therefore, we can just set

∂l\displaystyle\partial_{l} =min{GELU′(x)∣x∈[li,ui],[li,ui]=Di∩[l,u],i∈{1,2,3}}\displaystyle=\min~\left\{\gelu^{\prime}(x)\mid x\in[l_{i},u_{i}],~[l_{i},u_{i}]=D_{i}\cap[l,u],~i\in\{1,2,3\}\right\} (18)
∂u\displaystyle\partial_{u} =max{GELU′(x)∣x∈[li,ui],[li,ui]=Di∩[l,u],i∈{1,2,3}}.\displaystyle=\max~\left\{\gelu^{\prime}(x)\mid x\in[l_{i},u_{i}],~[l_{i},u_{i}]=D_{i}\cap[l,u],~i\in\{1,2,3\}\right\}\;. (19)

G.3 Increased Precision using Construction-time Verified Ranges

Note that the formulas to compute the neuron-wise differences (Equations (15),(17)) still partially depend on the values 𝐲i(l−1)\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}_{i}^{(l-1)} and 𝐲~i(l)\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mathbf{y}}}_{i}^{(l)} of neurons in the individual networks 𝒩1\net_{1} and 𝒩2\net_{2}. Our differential verification approach extends VeryDiff [23], which computes neuron ranges based on zonotope propagation and is thus limited to linear relaxations with parallel slopes. State-of-the-art NN verifiers like α\alpha-CROWN [24] are known to compute tighter bounds for ranges in single neural networks. If such a NN verifier was used to compute the verified pre-activation bounds of the polynomial network, we can use the tightened lower and upper bounds

l=max⁡{lz​o​n​o,lp},u=min⁡{uz​o​n​o,up},\displaystyle l=\max\{l_{zono},l_{p}\},~\quad u=\min\{u_{zono},u_{p}\}\;, (20)

where [lz​o​n​o,uz​o​n​o][l_{zono},u_{zono}] are the ranges computed by VeryDiff and [lp,up][l_{p},u_{p}] are the verified ranges for the polynomial network.

Appendix H Additional Evaluation Results

In this appendix, we provide a more detailed description of our benchmarks and base neural networks. Furthermore, we present additional evalation results.

H.1 Experiment Settings

We implemented our approach for certified design of polynomial neural networks in Julia [73] on top of the differential verification framework VeryDiff [23]. Execution of the polynomial networks under CKKS is based on OpenFHE [17].

To compute verified pre-activation ranges, we leverage the state-of-the-art NN verifier α\alpha-CROWN [24].

We use a piecewise-polynomial overapproximation q⁡(x)q(x) for the GELU\gelu activation function with verified error |q⁡(x)−GELU⁡(x)|≤10−10|q(x)-\gelu(x)|\leq 10^{-10}. The overapproximation uses 66 polynomial pieces of degree 1515 in addition to the linear asymptotes.

H.2 Benchmarks

We give a brief description of each dataset, the associated machine learning task and the training procedure of the neural networks for this benchmark. The network architectures for each benchmark are summarized in Table 5. All of the networks listed in this table are later used as base networks that are approximated by polynomial networks. As prior work [14] has already shown that training the base networks with L1L_{1}-regularization significantly reduces the polynomial approximation error, we only consider networks trained with L1L_{1}-penalty. Note that we use two networks for each listed architecture: One with ReLU\relu activation and one with GELU\gelu activation function.

We run our approach on benchmarks related to classification tasks to evaluate the difference in accuracy between base and polynomial network, and also evaluate on regression tasks, where the verified error bounds are a more meaningful measure for comparison between the base and the polynomial network.

H.2.1 Classification Benchmarks

HELOC. The home equity line of credit dataset [30] contains 2323 features used to predict if a person is credit-worthy. Following the procedure of prior work on certified construction of polynomial networks [14], we normalized the features to [0,1][0,1]. We also use the ReLU\relu neural networks provided by them. Neural networks with GELU\gelu activation are obtained by training directly on the HELOC dataset.

MNIST. Neural networks trained on the MNIST dataset [74] aim to correctly classify the handwritten digit shown on 28×2828\times 28 pixel grayscale images. Pixel values are normalized to [0,1][0,1]. Since Kern et al. [14] also evaluated on MNIST, we simply reuse their ReLU\relu networks. Additionally, we train networks of the same architecture with GELU\gelu activation on the MNIST dataset to obtain base networks with this activation function.

CIFAR10. The task associated with the CIFAR10 dataset [32] is to assign the correct labels to images represented by inputs of dimension 3×32×323\times 32\times 32, where each dimension can attain values in [0,1][0,1]. The dataset is a popular benchmark used to evaluate FHE neural networks [65, 12]. However, those approaches rely on sampled pre-activation bounds. To achieve good accuracy of the polynomial networks – despite wide verified bounds due to overapproximation incurred for large networks by NN verifiers – we train two convolutional networks of different sizes ourselves. The difference in performance between the small and the large network can then be used to judge scalability of our verified approach.

H.2.2 Regression Benchmarks

Residential Electricity Forecasting (EC). Prior research on FHE used electricity demand forecasting as a use case [75]. In such setting, the smart meter associated to a residential building would send encrypted consumption data to a centralised server and get a short-term (half-hour) prediction of the future load. Similar to [75], we train a network that receives the past 24 hours of consumption data as input (averaged across 1010 homes), and predicts the next half-hour consumption. Additional input features include day of the year, day of the week, and time of the day. The dataset is real-world consumption data from a large-scale study from 2011, Ireland [31]. As discovered by [76], a small fully-connected network with a single hidden layer suffice to maximise predictive accuracy; we choose a width of 6464 neurons.

NN4Sys. We use the learned index models from the NN4Sys benchmark [33] used in the annual neural network verification competition VNNComp [35]. The associated task is, to map a key (a scalar in [0,1][0,1]) to an index (also a scalar in [0,1][0,1]) in a database. Since the available networks are not trained using L1L_{1} regularization, we extract a training dataset from the input-output specifications that were used in the competition to train r​e​l​urelu and g​e​l​ugelu neural networks from scratch. We use the same architecture as the non-L1L_{1} regularized networks in the original NN4Sys benchmark.

Collins RUL. The Collins RUL benchmark [34] was also used in the competition VNNComp [35]. It consists of convolutional networks that process multivariate time series data (windows of 2020 time steps for 2020 sensors) to predict the remaining useful life of aircraft components. Since the original networks provided by the benchmark are, again, not trained using L1L_{1} regularization, we train ReLU\relu and GELU\gelu networks of the same structure ourselves. However, as the benchmark is only accompanied by a small test dataset, we train our networks to minimize the mean squared error (𝒩L1⁡(x)−𝒩⁡(x))2(\net_{L_{1}}(x)-\net(x))^{2} to the original network over random data (while monitoring the loss over the test dataset).

H.3 Additional Examples for Overflow Attacks

Four examples of inputs triggering overflows in the polynomial CIFAR10 network constructed using sampling-based bounds, were already shown in Figure 1.

Here, we show additional examples of such inputs for the CIFAR10 network are shown in Figure 11.

Examples for the MNIST case can be found in Figure 9.

H.4 Extended Ablation Results

As shown in Figure 10(a), runtime increases for larger polynomial degrees as computation of roots is more expensive. However, there is a large fixed cost related to the runtime of the NN verifier which scales in the size of the network.

H.5 Extended Results for Certified Design at Scale

In Table 6, we provide an extended version of Table 2 shown in Section 5.3. We additionally compare to base networks with ReLU\relu activation and their polynomial approximations. Furthermore, we report results on a wider range of network architectures.

It is evident that the verified bound on the approximation error is much smaller for the base networks with GELU\gelu activation than for the ReLU\relu networks. While classification performance is not affected (and is even better for for the large ReLU\relu CIFAR10 network than the GELU\gelu network at degree 119119), the MSE loss for the NN4Sys benchmark is significantly worse for the ReLU\relu networks.

It is also worth pointing out that the verified bounds on the approximation error are very tight for the HELOC, MNIST, EC and NN4Sys GELU\gelu networks and still useful for even the large Collins RUL GELU\gelu network – considering its wide sampled output range over the dataset.
